The Comanche (/kəˈmæntʃi/), or Nʉmʉnʉʉ (Comanche: Nʉmʉnʉʉ, 'the people'), are a Native American people from the Southern Plains of the present-day United States. Comanche people today primarily belong to the federally recognized Comanche Nation, headquartered in Lawton, Oklahoma.
The Comanche language is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family. Originally, it was a Shoshoni dialect, but diverged and became a separate language. The Comanche were once part of the Shoshone people of the Great Basin, diverging linguistically and culturally after adopting a nomadic horse culture in the early 18th century.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, the Comanche became renowned as some of the finest cavalry in history, utilising mobility and bison hunting to build a vast sovereign territory across present-day northwestern Texas, eastern New Mexico, southeastern Colorado, southwestern Kansas, and western Oklahoma - an empire known to colonists as Comanchería. Rather than a single centralized state, Comanche society operated through politically autonomous divisions linked by kinship. At their peak, the Comanche language was the lingua franca of the southern Great Plains region.

The Comanche commanded a complex web of diplomacy, trade, and conflict with neighboring Native American nations, European powers, and American settlers. Especially noteworthy were their large-scale raids in the 1840s and 1850s, which penetrated hundreds of miles into Mexico to capture livestock they mostly sold to Anglo-Americans in Texas. They also took many captives, using them as slaves, selling them to the Spanish and (later) to Mexican settlers, or adopting them into their tribe. Thousands of captives from raids, as well as entire Native American groups were assimilated into Comanche society. Epidemics of diseases, destruction of the bison herds, and warfare and massacres by the U.S. army forced the Comanche onto reservations in Indian Territory in the mid-1870s.
